title: Grace before meals
hookLine: bless us, O Lord, and these thy gifts

lines: SAID IN THE TIME STEAM RISES.
cards: Tuesday night. Spaghetti, again. A seven-year-old has his fork halfway to his mouth when his grandmother clears her throat.
He freezes, puts the fork down, and sighs. Everyone makes the sign of the cross, some faster than others. Then, together, in about the time it takes the steam to rise off the plates, they say it.
Bless us, O Lord, and these thy gifts, which we are about to receive from thy bounty, through Christ our Lord. Amen. Fork back up.
Someone asks for the parmesan. It's over so fast it's easy to miss what was just said.

teach.b: That's the table grace in a traditional English form. You met it in your second week, at a grandmother's table. Today, slowly: four short phrases.
First, bless us. Not the food first. The people: the ones at the table, tired, hungry, maybe annoyed with each other.
Second, these thy gifts. The spaghetti was bought at a store, cooked by someone's tired hands, paid for with someone's work. All true.
And the prayer still calls it a gift, from God, before it's anything else. It quietly rearranges the plate. Third, which we are about to receive.
Receive, not take. You can't earn a gift; you can only accept it.

teach.h: HE LOOKED UP, BLESSED, AND BROKE.
teach.b: And from thy bounty: from God's generosity, which is bigger than this meal. Fourth, through Christ our Lord. The prayer goes through Jesus, who did this himself.
In Mark's Gospel, a huge hungry crowd has followed him into a deserted place, and the disciples want to send them away to buy food.
Instead he takes five loaves and two fishes, looks up to heaven, blesses, breaks the loaves, and gives them to be shared.
Everyone eats. Some readers see grace at the table as copying that gesture: look up, bless, then share. Some families add grace after meals too, a short thanks when the plates are empty.
Before or after, the point is the same. The food was a gift.

how: Catholic families make the sign of the cross and say the traditional grace, "Bless us, O Lord, and these thy gifts," together before meals at home and sometimes in restaurants; some also say a grace after meals.

o: thanks said only at Christmas and Easter dinners
a rule against eating before the priest arrives
a short table prayer calling the food God's gift

games.q: grace before meals — tap the pairs.
p: the people first, then the food
a gift is received, not taken

s: the prayer asks God to bless the food first
it begins with bless us: the people at the table come first.
in Mark's Gospel Jesus looks up to heaven and blesses the loaves before sharing them
he looks up, blesses, breaks and gives them to be shared with the crowd.
calling food a gift means nobody worked for it
it was grown, bought and cooked by real hands. the prayer still calls it a gift from God first.

games.q: you're a disciple. a huge, hungry crowd has followed Jesus into a deserted place and it's late. you tell him to send them away to buy food. what does he do?
o: agrees, and sends them to the villages.
takes five loaves and two fishes, looks up, blesses, breaks and gives.
tells the crowd to fast until morning.
games.why: he blesses what little there is, breaks it, and has it shared. everyone eats. grace at the table copies that gesture.

practice: Picture the next thing you'll eat, a sandwich at a desk, a bowl of cereal, dinner with people you love, and the hands it passed through: the grower, the driver, the cook. Then picture pausing for one breath before the first bite.
If you pray, say the grace slowly, letting each phrase land; if you don't, just pause and notice where the food came from.

wordCard.voice: Grace before meals. A short blessing said at the table, asking God to bless the people and calling the food his gift. Today's word.
